speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising from the suspicion of fraud and other irregularities in the letting of Olympic contracts, resulting in police raids on the builders of the Olympic Village, and continuing exorbitant and irregular expenditures by Montreal and COJO of funds generated by federally backed legislation. subsubtopic: CONTRACT TO LOCKHEED FOR LONG-RANGE PATROL AIRCRAFT-OTHER OPTIONS OPEN TO GOVERNMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Prime Minister arising from the $950 purchase which the Department of National Defence is making from the Lockheed Aircraft Corporation for the replacement of the Argus. In view of the fact that there have been reports that other companies such as Boeing Aircraft, and the Douglas Corporation have placed before the government various package deals which would result in a larger percentage of the money spent going to Canadian aircraft companies, I want to ask the Prime Minister what options were open to the government when they made the decision to grant the contract to Lockheed Corporation.

subsubtopic: CONTRACT TO LOCKHEED FOR LONG-RANGE PATROL AIRCRAFT-OTHER OPTIONS OPEN TO GOVERNMENT

details are concerned I would urge the hon. member to address his question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce when my colleague is here because it was principally his department which had the responsibility of studying the various options from the point of view of the industrial fall-outs for Canada, the offsets, the value of them, and so on. I am sure that within the bounds of whatever secrecy is involved in the bids by the companies, the minister would be more helpful than I. Are the reports on Wednesday that he is considering a very sharp change in the government's program of support for multiculturalism true, and will the new programs mean a downgrading of the grants which have been given to the ethnic communities which they already consider to be too little too late, and does it include a rejection of federal support for the teaching of languages other than English or French?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF ALLEGED CHANGE IN POLICY-DISCUSSION WITH CONSULTATIVE COUNCIL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad that the hon. member has asked that question because it affords me the opportunity to clarify the situation. No, it is not a downgrading of the concept of multiculturalism, nor is it a downgrading of the grants to various ethno-cultural groups in Canada. What it is, what we are thinking about and what I have discussed with various ethno-cultural groups, including the Ukrainian community in Montreal, is whether it would not be worth considering shifting the emphasis in terms of combatting discrimination and breaking down some barriers which some of the minority groups and ethno-cultural groups are experiencing without withdrawing assistance to all ethno-cultural groups. The reaction I have been receiving has been positive, and it was in that context that I have been discussing this change of emphasis. I think, as the previous minister of multiculturalism will attest, it has always been an element of the multicultural policy to promote understanding and combat discrimination.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF ALLEGED CHANGE IN POLICY-DISCUSSION WITH CONSULTATIVE COUNCIL
speechtext:
Due to the fact that the combatting of discrimination has been traditionally part of the work done by other departments of the federal government, such as the Department of the Secretary of State, the Department of Labour and the provincial governments, and in view of fact that the minister's change in policy or change in emphasis does not seem to have been discussed at least 
with the chairman of the Canadian Consultative Council on Multiculturalism, Mr. Koteles, who expressed shock when he heard of the minister's changed policy, can the minister explain whether his new approach has been discussed with the organization which the government itself set up to advise it on the kind of work which the government should be supporting?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF ALLEGED CHANGE IN POLICY-DISCUSSION WITH CONSULTATIVE COUNCIL
speechtext:
I would advise the hon. member that I have been attending various meetings of the Canadian Consultative Council on Multiculturalism and regional meetings. We have been discussing the various elements of the whole policy in terms of a review that I wanted to take forward to the government fairly soon. These discussions have been public in nature; there is no question about that. In terms of asking questions with respect to the direction of policy, I have already mentioned to you that I have done it with various groups. It seemed to have been well received by various groups. I cannot accept responsibility for Mr. Koteles, he will have to accept that on his own responsibility.
As far as teaching of third languages or, if you like, retention of languages, that has always been an element of the policy. We will continue to offer grants in that connection on the assumption and hope that it will be an instrument in itself to combat discrimination and to attain any understanding between ethno-cultural groups as well as to assist all Canadians in appreciating the contribution these cultural groups make to Canada.

subsubtopic: ANGOLA-POSSIBILITY OF PROTEST OF RUSSIAN INTERFERENCE IN CIVIL STRIFE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs and concerns that section of the Helsinki accord which was referred to earlier today, in particular-section VIII which reads as follows:
... all peoples always have the right, in full freedom, to determine, when and as they wish, their internal and external political status, without external interference,-
I bring to his attention the situation dangerous to world peace in Angola in which the U.S.S.R. flagrantly is breaking this section of the accord, either directly or indirectly, by puppets operating under its tutelage. Has the Canadian government protested to the government of the U.S.S.R. that this is wrong or does it intend to bring it before the United Nations? There is nothing more dangerous to world peace than what is occurring at the present time over there.

subsubtopic: ANGOLA-POSSIBILITY OF PROTEST OF RUSSIAN INTERFERENCE IN CIVIL STRIFE

We have not made the direct approach of protest
November 28, 1975

to the Soviet government at this point but we have made our position quite clear at the United Nations where all countries know where we stand.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel Roy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):

subsubtopic: CHEESE IMPORTS
speechtext:
1. Cheese of all types have been on the import control list of the Export and Import Permits Act for the past five years. During this period, import permits were freely issued for all cheese imported for direct consumption except cheddar and colby. On June 6, 1975, a global import quota for all types of cheese was established. The quota amounts to 50 million pounds for 1975 and represents an increase of 2 million pounds over 1974 imports. The size of the quota was determined by taking into account the requirements of the Canadian market, recent performance of imports and the relationship of imports to the domestic dairy situation.
2.	Canadian cheeses supply 84 per cent of the domestic market. Cheese imports provide a wider selection of cheese to consumers as many of the cheeses imported are not manufactured in Canada. It is recognized by the cheese industry that the wide variety of imported cheese has stimulated consumer interest in cheese. This has been a major factor for increasing the consumption of all types of cheese.
3.	The retail prices of imported and domestic cheese are not monitored and statistics on comparative prices are not available. However, it is estimated that 50 per cent of imported cheeses retail at prices above domestic cheese and 50 per cent of cheese imports retail at prices competitive with Canadian cheeses.

subsubtopic: 'SOCIAL SECURITY
speechtext:
1.	Have any countries during the years 1973, 1974 or 1975 expressed an interest in concluding a reciprocal agreement with Canada in respect of social security and, if so, which countries and, in each case, with respect to what branches of social security?
2.	Are negotiations in progress with any of such countries looking toward a social security reciprocal agreement and, if so, which ones?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: 'SOCIAL SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is as follows. 1. During the years 1973, 1974 or 1975, Belgium, Bermuda, Guyana, Italy, Jamaica, Malta, Norway, the United Kingdom and the United States of America respectively have expressed an interest in concluding a reciprocal agreement with Canada with respect to one or more of the following branches of social security: Old Age, Invalidity, Survivors and Death; Sickness and Maternity; Work Injury; Unemployment; and Family Allowances.
2. Although technical discussions have been held with the United Kingdom, the United States of America and Italy, no formal negotiations have taken place with any of the countries interested in concluding such an agreement. Informal contacts, however, have been maintained. For

example, this subject was discussed in general terms in a most cordial and welcome visit this morning among the minister, myself and the new Italian ambassador, His Excellency, Giorgio Smoquina.

speechtext: Is it normal that a postal parcel without any market value, sent by air cargo from New York to Montreal, be subject, in addition to transportation fees, to custom clearance fees when it is taken in charge by the addressee and, if so (a) for what reason (b) does the government intend to apply the same rule with respect to travellers entering Canada and taking possession of their luggage at Canadian customs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack Cullen (Minister of National Revenue):
subsubtopic: 'CUSTOMS CLEARANCE FEES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer is as follows; (a) Canada Customs does not levy a fee for clearance of postal parcels into Canada during authorized hours of customs business, other than duties and taxes. subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on motion No. 5 to Bill C-41 respecting the stabilization of western grains. I am going to support this motion, which adds the following provisions to the bill.
(i)	depreciation on farm machinery and equipment used for grain
November 28, 1975

production or used in the farm business in respect of grain production and transportation;
(j)	interest charges incurred in respect of the production or sale of grain; and
(k)	producer levies in respect of this act.
These are to be added to the cost of production for the purpose of the Western Grain Stabilization Act. I am sure almost every member of this House will agree that interest and depreciation can be one of the larger costs of production. If we were going through this type of exercise of stabilization in business and in industry they would be very much in favour of including interest charges and depreciation in their costs. Interest is, of course, a real cost. In my opinion it must be included in any cost of production, whether it be farm, business or industry.
I want to speak about interest for a short while, and farm loans, especially those made to young farmers. The government has taken a good step forward in increasing the amount of these loans so that young farmers can more easily get into the business of farming. This is what we need in Canada-more young farmers. It has been shown that the average age of farmers is high. Therefore, as I say, more young farmers are needed. When a farmer goes to the farm loan people to get a loan, I am sure one of the main things they look at is the interest cost; how much interest he is paying on the farm machinery which he needs to operate his business properly.
When we look at stabilization bills we find the government does not believe interest rates should be counted as part of the costs of production. We went through all this in connection whith the stabilization bill which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) presented to us. Hon. members may recall that the Federation of Agriculture along with other farm organizations, made strong representations to the minister pointing out that interest charges represented a real cost and one which should be taken into consideration.
Consider what is happening to farming in Canada. Farming has become highly mechanized. The Minister of Agriculture himself pointed but that as a result of mechanization, farmers produce more than any other workers in Canada. This was made possible because of moving from a highly labour-intensive industry to a highly mechanized industry. In order to do this, of course, farmers had to borrow money, thus incurring interest charges which have been running at increasingly high rates. It is true that machines are labour-saving, but they represent a serious investment for the farmer concerned, and if we turn our backs on costs of this type when we consider any kind of stabilization bill, we are acting incorrectly.
If we follow this argument through, we find that depreciation becomes a more important factor than ever because of the high initial cost of farm machinery. Possession of one machine creates the need for another to complement the one you already have; the farmer immediately finds himself dependent on a series of costly machines and his concern about their depreciation is increased accordingly. While we are on the subject of depreciation, allow me to quote what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Goodale) said yesterday in
Grain Stabilization
response to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). Speaking on motion No. 5, he said:
There can be no doubt that if you were to ask a producer a very blunt and straightforward question about what he views as being one of his most important cost items he would probably reply that it was depreciation. It was not very long ago that western grain producers were literally living off their depreciation. It is an item which is first and foremost on their minds. When one looks at the particular provision in the context of the grains stabilization bill, one can see that the inclusion of depreciation is not one that will enhance the protection this bill offers western grain producers.
That is quite a statement. Ask any farmer whether he agrees with it. The only part I agree with is that farmers have sometimes had to live off the depreciation on their machinery. They did not want to do so because it is not a good position to be in. However, farmers in Canada were sometimes obliged to do it because they were not getting their cost of production, or enough money to live on, out of the market. It did not enhance their operation, because what they were doing was taking out the money they should have been using to replace their machinery.
What happens when farmers do not have the money to buy new machinery? They borrow more money for that purpose, thus increasing their debt and incurring further interest costs, which in turn means a higher cost of production. They are not using their depreciation allowance in the manner in which it is supposed to be used. The statement the parliamentary secretary made shows he knows very little, or nothing, about farming or about what farmers have to go through. The depreciation provisions are there to enable a farmer to replace his machines. They are a legitimate cost for which provision is made by the Department of National Revenue. This applies to farmers, to businessmen and to everyone else. The commercial world could not operate properly without it.
It would, of course, be very nice to be able to buy a machine and to write off its cost in the first year. But that is not the way in which the system is set up. As it is, the purchase becomes a legitimate cost of production in the total operation of the farm. Today, as I have explained, it is even more important than it was in the past. The parliamentary secretary was saying, in effect, the farmers are buying machinery so they can live off the depreciation, or else that farmers are overmechanized. Let me tell him that no farmer who buys more machinery than he needs, just to live off the depreciation will last very long. He should be using his depreciation allowance correctly so that he can replace his machinery as it wears out.
There is also the argument that farm machinery is in the nature of a long-term investment. A farmer uses his machines as long as he can; he does not dispose of them until they are worn out or have been superseded by other types which are much more efficient and cut down his costs of production. Anyone experienced in farming knows that many of the machines farmers buy do not last very long; they do not have a long life. Every hon. member knows about the life of a car and how long it can be kept before being traded in. Farm machinery suffers more abuse than cars, and as a result its life is short.
The minister used some examples showing western farmers what the stabilization act did between 1954 and

November 28, 1975
Grain Stabilization
1974, a period of 20 years. Not too many machines last for 20 years. They are more likely to wear out or have to be replaced within five years. It is not very often that you can fully depreciate a machine under the Income Tax Act before it is worn out.
I very much support the amendment which seeks to include depreciation in the cost of production. In addition, the amendment seeks to have producer levies included in the act. Once again, this is a very real cost of production for farmers. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport in his speech yesterday said they were going to be included, but if I heard correctly in committee I got an entirely different interpretation; I understood they were not going to be included in the cost of production. Even though it has been said that producer levies are to be included, this has yet to be determined. Certainly it is something that should be included in the motion.
When the agriculture committee toured the three prairie provinces to hear briefs on the stabilization bill and to talk to farmers, I did not talk to one farmer who told me that depreciation, interest and levies should not be included in the cost of production. Quite frankly, we did not find too many farmers hotly in favour of the stabilization bill, but nevertheless they said that if parliament imposed it upon them, they wanted everything included that it was proper to include. This is the reason I have taken a few minutes of the time of the House to speak to this motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have very few comments to summarize the arguments on the government side of the House against motion No. 5 which has been debated rather extensively. As well, perhaps, I make the request for understanding on the part of the non-agricultural members of the House. This is a comprehensive bill which is of great import to western Canada. The measure has taken a good deal of time.
I should like to correct a misunderstanding that has been left-I say a misunderstanding rather than a misstatement-by my colleague, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale), who discussed this amendment in the House last night. Hon. members will find his speech reported at page 9527 of Hansard. Essentially, the remarks of my colleague from Assiniboia were correct with respect to paragraph (c)(i) of the motion we are debating, namely, whether or not to include depreciation. The hon. member for Assiniboia was also correct so far as paragraph (c) (j) was concerned respecting interest charges. Where the misunderstanding came about was in the hon. member's remarks that dealt with the inclusion of producer levies in this legislation.
I suppose that clause 8(3)(f), insurance premiums, at page 11 of the bill could be interpreted to include producer levies, and that was the understanding of the hon. member for Assiniboia. However, both he and I checked with the minister and his departmental officials, and that is not the interpretation to be made of that provision. In other words, producer levies are not now included within the term "insurance premiums". Part of the logic here makes sense, in that if producer levies were added as part of the cost, you would then have to consider any pay-outs that may be triggered by the bill as income, on the other side of the coin. While producer levies are not included as an expense
|Mr. Whittaker.]
under this provision in the act so far as area gross expenses are concerned, it is a deductible expense for income tax purposes for any individual farmer making payment.
I could spend some time responding to the remarks of the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) about depreciation. Certainly he does not have to convince any member on this side that it is indeed a very real cost. The idea of including depreciation in some way in the bill has been explored and examined pretty thoroughly. To come back to the point made by my hon. friends opposite, at the moment this bill is fairly complicated and it was felt that it would be complicated further by including depreciation, without bringing about the desired kind of action or response in terms of the plan itself. I can only inform hon. members that the officials were able to convince me that it was wise to leave it out. We are not saying that it is not an expense, but from the point of view of the bill it was felt it was better to leave it out. With these few words, I hope I have been able to clarify one misunderstanding that was left in the debate last night regarding producer levies being included as an expense.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to add some words in general agreement of the suggestion that some parts of this amendment are worthy of acceptance, particularly as it concerns depreciation of farm machinery. In the case of any farmer in western Canada, particularly a new producer or one who intends to farm for a number of years, most of his expenses are in farm machinery. I think it is significant that the value of his land is quite a bit less than the value of his farm machinery, compared to the situation 25 years ago. This means that the cost of farming has increased rapidly because of rapid increases in the price of farm machinery.
I think it should be realized that the market for farm machinery is continent-wide in North America and that the guidelines in respect of control may well have an effect, but the price of farm machinery will continue to rise. We have seen rapid increases in the price of farm machinery. We have seen the price of a tractor increase from $10,000 to $20,000 in a period of two or three years. If we take any fairly recent farm operation, say in the last five or six years, we may find that the cost of the land is less than the cost of the machinery.
In this bill, apparently, repairs will be counted as an expense but depreciation will not be so counted. It is said this is because it would be difficult to administer. However, income tax returns could be used in a general way. Statistics regarding the sale of new farm machinery are compiled by Statistics Canada. With regard to practically every aspect of farm input there is general knowledge
Grain Stabilization
through the reporting by firms, and so on. If fertilizer and oil, for instance, may be computed in the cost of producing grain, surely depreciation on farm machinery on a global basis would be easy to arrive at. Therefore, in respect of depreciation I do not think there should be any greater error in a global assessment of the total cost of machinery than there would be in a global assessment of the total cost of fertilizer, oil, gas, repairs to buildings and repairs to machines.
I might add that interest charges certainly represent a very great cost of doing business. This is recognized by the income tax department. When one receives a loan from a bank the banker, in looking at the viability of the farm operation or any other operation, recognizes the cost of interest as a cost of doing business.
This act is something of an experiment. It is an attempt to change the various programs that have grown up over the years in order to stabilize the western grain industry. If this legislation is to be meaningful in the future and of any value in the establishment of guidelines, it will have to be changed. About 10 per cent or 20 per cent of the farmers already established will avail themselves of this legislation. If we leave out depreciation on farm machinery, we will be leaving out perhaps 25 per cent of the total cost of a farming operation in any one year. If we include the interest, we are probably looking at another 10 per cent or 15 per cent.
In fact, without the inclusion of these items the plan will be grossly deficient in respect of assessing the actual cost of growing grain, particularly for the individual farmer. In the future, obviously, if this is to come directly to the individual farmer the cost of depreciation and interest will be very important matters to him.

Motion No. 6.
That Bill C-41, an act respecting the stabilization of net proceeds from the production and sale of western grain and to amend certain statutes in consequence thereof, be amended in clause 10 by striking out lines 1 to 29 at page 15.
[The Acting Speaker (Mrs. Morin).]

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are putting forward this motion on the ground that payments from the fund ought not to be reduced after three successive years in which net income from grain was so bad that pay-outs were required. Obviously, that is not the time to reduce the amount of the pay-outs from 100 per cent to 90 per cent, because participants in the plan will be in pretty bad financial shape. There might be some logic in reducing payments when times are good.
The purpose of our amendment is to keep the level of support always at 100 per cent. It would strike out the provision which would reduce the level of payment to 90 per cent over the last five-year average when the fund has been in a deficit position for three years. This would serve to enhance the stabilization effect of the plan. I thought the government wished to do everything they could to ensure the very purpose of the legislation, namely, the stabilization of net grain income. Our amendment would have that effect. We believe payments should not be reduced when they are most needed. That is surely not the time to start picking on people who have already been kicked in the face by declining world markets, transportation problems or poor world prices. It is not the time to be reducing the stabilization effect of the program. Surely the pay-outs should be left at 100 per cent.
No doubt you could get into a situation where the fund would be in a deficit position, or have a slightly larger deficit than would be the case after three successive years of pay-outs, but there will be the good years so far as loans to the fund are concerned, and there will be a recovery in future years as a result of contributions by producers and government. We do not think it is fitting, fair or proper to start reducing the stabilizing effects of the plan after three successive bad years; we would like to see 100 per cent pay-outs.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
I should like to make a few comments in connection with the motion moved by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). We have examined it in detail, as well as the clause in the bill. What concerns the members of our party is this: we feel the bill should be as actuarially sound as possible. I can see the reason for inclusion in the bill of a clause that reduces the pay-out to farmers when the amount of interest owing exceeds one-third of the aggregate of the annual levies. If we examine the statistics given to us in committee by representatives of the government, we note that for the period 1954 to 1974 this clause would take effect in 13 years. It is also interesting to note that in that 20-year period, for seven of the years there was additional money required to be put into the fund by the government, which led to interest of some $210 million, being charged to the fund, all of which had to be repaid by the producers.
I do not think it is fair to the producer to burden him with high interest costs. It is not fair to the taxpayers of Canada to be called upon to lend this money to the fund. I think it proves the fallacy of the actual program, which is supposed to be an over-all program. The plan is triggered when the net income over a five-year period is less than the amount of income in the year. This is the reason we proposed in the committee hearings an individual program that would provide for the producer to pay into an
November 28, 1975

individual fund $2 for every $1 put in by the government. This type of individual program would never require any loan by the federal government and would mean that the producer would never have to pay interest. He would have complete control of the plan and be able to adjust his income annually. If he did not need the money, he would not withdraw it; if he did need the money, he could. Ultimately, he could use it as a form of retirement pension if he chose, in the years that he was farming, not to draw from the plan.
These are the basic reasons we are opposing the amendment of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. While we do not like this bill, we would like to see it kept as good a bill as possible and as actuarially sound as possible. To adopt the motion before the House at the present time would create problems which would deplete the plan and cause the individual producer to be faced with high interest charges, particularly if the historic figures between the years 1954 and 1974 were used.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a few words to this particular amendment. I completely concur with the comments made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) about the actuarial soundness of the plan. There are two provisions in the bill to ensure that the legislation is always kept reasonable and logical from that point of view.
The particular section of the bill to which this amendment pertains is one that affects the size of the potential payment out of the plan. The other provision in the bill to safeguard the soundness of the legislation is the one that is dealt with in motion No. 9 standing in the name of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). I think the comments of the hon. member for Moose Jaw relate very much to that motion as well; it is very much on the same theme. I thank him for making the points he did; I think they were completely sound and reasonable. It is important that the legislation be kept as actuarially sound as possible. The provisions written into the bill in the first place are designed to do this. Unfortunately, the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre would tend to take away from that and make the plan less sound.
I might point out in passing that if my reading of the past 20 years' experience is accurate-I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw referred to this indirectly-if the plan had been in place for the past 20 years, although we would have gone through some bad years and some bad times which would have necessitated adjustment of the levy rates, I do not think we would ever have got to the point where there was an actual reduction in the payments. There may have been one year, but no more than one. I think this demonstrates the reasonableness of this kind of provision. To delete or negate it, as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre has moved, would make the plan somewhat artificial and tend, in a distorting sort of way, to insulate the plan, indeed to insulate the prairies region from real and practical factors in the world of grain production that simply cannot be ignored. With those few remarks, I thank the hon. member for Moose Jaw for his comments and urge the House to defeat this amendment.
Grain Stabilization
Before I sit down, may I refer briefly to the comments made this morning by my hon. friend and colleague from Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) having to do with the matter we were discussing yesterday, producer levies, and whether or not they could be classified as insurance premiums within the wording of the legislation. I thank the hon. member for clarifying that matter on my behalf. I should also like to apologize to hon. members if I in any way misled them in the comments I made in the House yesterday evening. If there was a misinterpretation on my part, it was certainly unintentional.
May I also, at this time, thank the hon. member for Moose Jaw and the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre for drawing this item to my attention and for accepting so graciously the explanation given earlier today.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at this stage, before I speak, does the government representative have any explanation for these two motions?

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. Motions Nos. 7 and 8, in the name of the minister, have to do with a clause that was placed in the bill in the first place in response to the recommendations and suggestion of various farm organizations and spokesmen from western Canada. They have to do with a situation where a producer decides to opt out of the stabilization plan in other words, to exercise his option-and then at a later stage changes his mind, as is his right under the legislation, and decides to come back in.
The original draft of the legislation suggested that a producer could simply exercise his option in that way and immediately return to the plan as a full-time participant. Some producer organizations and others said that this was not fair. It was suggested that if a producer decided, in his own good judgment, that he wanted to opt out of the plan and then changed his mind, he should be free to do so but should not be able to re-enter the plan on a full-time basis the same as a farmer who had been in from the beginning and had toughed it out, if you like, through thick and thin, in good years and in bad.
That suggestion seemed to have merit, so we produced a clause which provides that a farmer re-entering the plan comes in, not as a full participant but as a conditional participant, meaning that if there is to be a payment made from the stabilization fund in the first three years after he has changed his mind, he will receive only 90 per cent of the payment which he received in the first three years. When the three years have expired, he will become a full-time participant as if he had been in from the beginning.
The amendments the minister is putting forward do nothing more than simplify the calculation of that 10 per cent value that is to be taken off the potential payment to a [Mr. Sharp.)
producer in that conditional category. The calculation, as hon. members opposite have taken some pains to point out, is rather complicated. The provisions proposed in these amendments make it a very straight-forward and rather direct deduction of 10 per cent, which is much simpler than the original calculation set out in the legislation. The royal recommendation which hon. members see printed with the motion is required because this payment has the potential of increasing the amount of money that would be paid by the treasury.
I suppose it is a matter of mathematics in comparing the calculation as originally proposed with the one we are proposing by way of this amendment to see where the additional dollars might come from; but in simplifying the formula, as we are doing in these two motions, there might be a chance that the payment out to a conditional participant would be slightly higher than under the more complicated formula. That is all these amendments do. They do not affect the actuarial soundness of the plan. The amendments, clearly, are very much in favour of the western grain producer.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) for his explanation. I support the view he has put forward. I think it points out what the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) mentioned earlier today, namely, that by placing this legislation in the area of a pay-out bill, whereby everyone knows what he pays in but does not know what he will receive in the form of a pay-out, we will run into the problems just described by the parliamentary secretary.
If we had a plan whereby each man put in his money and the federal government put its money into an individual plan, there would be no necessity for all these definitions and rules, we would have something much simpler to explairf to the farmers, and it would be easier to get the farmers into the plan. But no matter how hard one works on this type of legislation, it is so complicated that I am certain the selling job required to get the farmers to see the merit of the plan will be difficult.
These two amendments are a little fairer and, I would suggest, will add a burden to the treasury in that it may be paying out more than under the original statute. But in essence these amendments will make it easier to sell farmers the idea that they should get into the plan. We will support the government's amendments because they improve slightly what is very bad legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is a little ironic that when dealing with this bill, first of all the minister made some erroneous statements and then the parliamentary secretary made the same type of erroneous statements. Thank goodness we have the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) who can try to clarify those comments, but if the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley should make an erroneous statement, I wonder who would correct him.
This is a simple bill. I should like to read a portion of the clause so as to put on the record what we are dealing with here. It is very simple and I am sure the House leader will be very happy to agree that it is simple. Clause 12(b) reads as follows:

It is perfectly straightforward, understandable English. Is it any wonder that we find the minister is misinterpreting the provision, as is his parliamentary secretary? The ironical part of it is that, as a member of the House and formerly a grain producer in western Canada, I am very much aware of the fact that in order to stabilize the grain industry it is not necessary to bring in a complicated formula.
The parliamentary secretary to the minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Goodale) told us that the operation will only cost $300,000 a year. Why, then, do we have $300,000 in the present supplementary estimates with which we have to deal in the Standing Committee on Agriculture to cover the period from now until March 31? Also, we were told that probably other supplementary estimates would be coming before the committee prior to that time, so why is the whole amount included in the supplementary estimates if it is to apply to the whole period of 12 months? It seems to me that part of these estimates could be included in next year's estimates. I see the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley agrees with me on this, and it makes common sense.
One of our great concerns with this bill is that now another bureaucracy will have to be set up. We all know that the greater the bureaucracy, the more costly the operation for which eventually the taxpayers have to pay, which includes each and every one of us in the House. We are only trying to help the government to cut down their expenditures, but it is very difficult to get through to the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) and make him understand it is difficult for the taxpayer to have continually to increase the amount he is paying to the Department of National Revenue.
We have just been through the exercise, in western Canada, known as the PFAA which was primarily set up to achieve the same objectives as those for which the Prairie Grain Stabilization Act was set up. I believe that this whole program could be run from Ottawa. If you want to find exactly what the cost of the operation of any farm in western Canada is, all you have to do is accumulate the total cost to the Department of National Revenue. Certainly, in this age of computers, it should not be difficult to do. Then average out the cost and, using figures from Statistics Canada on whatever increase there may be in production, you will arrive at a figure which will give you the cost factor acceptable to the producer and which will be of benefit to the government.
Grain Stabilization
It seems to me that this is a simple method of finding out the cost. If we cut down the cost, we will increase the return to the producer. I feel that there has been an oversight on the part of the minister and of his supporting staff in that they did not bring out a simple formula whereby the producers would know what they will receive in certain years when their income is lower.
The parliamentary secretary mentioned that those who opt out of the program and later come back in will be penalized. This is why we have the amendments that are before us at present. I agree that certain penalties should be established for opting out and then coming back in, as the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) suggested, but if the program is acceptable and benefits the producers, they will want to stay in it.
The value of this program is being questioned by western producers. Many of them feel they can take it or leave it; they couldn't care less. When you talk to people out there, you find they are not very interested in the program, primarily because they do not think it will be of much value to them. One of the great shortcomings of the program is that it brings no return to the individual who, after making premium payments for several years, decides to leave farming. That is one of the reasons older farmers do not wish to participate in the program. They cannot afford to take a chance on not getting any return on the premiums they have paid. Why should they pay into a program for three, four or five years, then leave farming and have no return whatsoever? There are other people who do not want to take a chance on participating in the program because they fear because they will not get any return on the money they pay in.
This is not an acceptable program, and what I regret is that it will probably take the place of what could be an acceptable program some time in the future. It is always very difficult to change these schemes once they are put in place. After a producer pays into a program for five, six or even ten years, if a new one is brought in surely he should not lose the money he paid under the first program. Farmers should not be penalized because new programs are introduced. Once a producer participates in a program, it becomes very difficult to bring in another sound, acceptable one. Provision must be made in any new program which will make it acceptable to the producers.
That is why I believe the minister and his parliamentary secretary have short-changed the western prairie grain producers in this bill, although they had a golden opportunity - probably there will never be a similar opportunity for years-to bring in an acceptable program which would be of benefit to producers, one that they would want. As I said earlier, if you speak to the producers you will find that many of them couldn't care less. What can we in the opposition do? We have to support this bill because there is no better program to support at this time. Surely somewhere down the road we will have the opportunity of establishing a program for the grain producers which will be of benefit to them and, ultimately, to Canadian taxpayers.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) and pleased that he took the time to read one of the sections of the bill to put on the public record its complicated nature. It is all very well to have statute books, but not too many people, except lawyers, read the statutes. When something like this is recorded in Hansard, however, it gets very wide public coverage.
On two or three occasions I have asked friends of mine in the legal profession to look over certain sections of the bill and, like me, they found many of them almost incomprehensible. Our committee travelled for one week last summer in western Canada. We went to the three prairie provinces, to the major cities, accepted briefs and heard presentations by various farm organizations, such as the wheat pools and the Palliser group and others. Almost every organization that presented a brief spoke of the complexity of the legislation. It had been placed in their hands a considerable time before, and I understand that a briefing team from the Department of Agriculture travelled to western Canada to meet with executives of the farm organizations. Those executives told us that despite the briefing they still thought the bill was so difficult and complex that they were not able to cummunicate with their grass roots people in order to get an expression of opinion from them.
I think it is important that producers in Canadian Wheat Board regions understand what the legislation is about. If they do not understand it, they are certainly not going to participate.
It is important that the government put out a brochure on this bill, explaining it in layman's terms so that farmers will know what their contributions will be as well as the government's contributions, and they will know the penalties if they decide to opt out of the program and then opt into it. If that is not done, I am afraid a great many producers in western Canada will not participate in the plan, and unless the majority participate it will not work. Despite what I have just said, I am afraid that even with explanations the producers of western Canada will not accept the plan as satisfactory.
I mentioned earlier today, and I want to repeat it, that we on this side believe in a program of individual participation. We submitted a fairly comprehensive paper to the committee setting out in detail what our program was. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board did not see fit to accept our proposals. He said that perhaps some time in the future such an individual plan could be worked out, but in the meantime he was going to proceed with the complicated piece of legislation that we have before us. We suggested that perhaps the legislation could be delayed and, after further consultation with representatives of the producers in western Canada, a satisfactory plan could be worked out. He did not see fit to do that; consequently, we are faced with this legislation which will shortly become law.
As far as the amendment is concerned, it is to a very complicated clause and I accept the explanation of the hon. member for Assiniboia as to its intent. I shall leave it at that.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment and another one we submitted were an effort to reverse some of the backward provisions of the legislation. The legislation rewards fortune and penalizes misfortune. Those who have the highest income in the year of the pay-out get the highest pay-out; those with the lowest income in the year of the pay-out get the lowest pay-out. That has to be a backward principle.
Similarly, years of a deficit positions for the fund will obviously be years when grain producers are in the worst possible circumstances, or there would not be pay-outs to
November 28, 1975

cause deficits in the fund. Obviously, they are not in a financial position then to be assessed extra charges for expenses or anything else. What the government proposes to do in years of financial difficulty when the grain and income stabilization fund is in deficit is to increase the levy. That is the worst possible time for them to be paying out more money, so the purpose of the amendment is to make the levy a constant 2 per cent.
Variability based on the fund's surplus or deficit position could have a destabilizing effect contrary to the intention and purpose of the legislation, which is to stabilize. To reduce the levy when the fund is in surplus means the grain producers are in good financial shape, but that is when they can afford to pay a higher levy. When the fund is in deficit and farmers cannot afford the extra cost, the government proposes to raise the levy. Really, that is when farmers cannot afford to pay extra money for anything. That is when farmers will be in the worst position. This proposal is therefore backward.
Would it not be more logical to increase the levy when the fund is in surplus, thereby making the surplus even larger, so that when farmers draw on the fund in adverse years it will not go into deficit? Farmers, I am sure, would be willing to pay higher levies in good years and build up big reserves which will earn interest and further swell the fund, so that in bad years payments out can be made from the fund without incurring any deficit. The farmers could draw on the reserves which had increased in good years and to which both the producer and the government has contributed. You should not call on the producer to pay more into the fund at the worst possible time, when the fund is in deficit. If a fellow has been kicked in the face, why add to his troubles?
Why can we not turn this proposal around? Let the government accept half a dozen amendments which would make certain that a good principle is not applied backwards; I will put it that way. I would much rather the bill provided for levies to be higher in good years so that surpluses could be increased. It is time we built up our reserves so that when the fund is drawn on in bad years it will not be necessary to increase levies.
If I cannot persuade my colleagues on all sides to support my suggestion, I hope at least they will agree to allow the 2 per cent levy to remain constant. Two per cent should be the constant rate, at least until we have had several years' experience with the collection of levies and the government's contributions. After we gain experience with the workings of the fund and know whether the level of contributions is sufficient or insufficient, it will be possible for the government to come before the House and say, "We must make the following changes, based on experience." The present proposal calls on producers to make larger contributions to the fund when they can least afford to do so. I hope this motion commends itself to colleagues on all sides. I hope the minister likes what I propose and accepts the amendment, as that will save time, to the great relief of the government House leader.

Mr. Speaker, I have examined the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). He said, I think, that
Grain Stabilization
his amendment would not turn around the provisions of the clause being discussed, although that is what he would like to do. Perhaps if he had introduced an amendment of that kind, my party could have taken a hard look at it and considered supporting it.
Basically, the clause as it now reads provides for a levy of 2 per cent on grain sales up to $25,000 under normal circumstances. The balance of the clause, which the hon. member proposes to amend with a deletion, would reduce the levy from 2 per cent to 1.5 per cent in any year when the interest to the credit of the producer exceeds one-third of that annual levy. Later there is provision for reducing the levy to 1 per cent. The final portion of the clause would increase the levy to 2.5 per cent in years when the interest charged to the fund by the government for moneys lent to the plan exceeds one-third of the annual levy. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre proposes to fix the rate at 2 per cent, without variation. He suggests this will not create hardship for producers, as in years when the crop is good they should pay a higher levy, and in years when the crop is bad, a lower levy.
Possibly his suggestion has merit. On the other hand, he proposes a reduction of one-half of 1 per cent which, in concrete terms, involves at most the sum of $125 in a year in which the producer sells $25,000 worth of grain. In these circumstances, I feel members of my party cannot support this motion. I hope the government will take a hard look at the bill in the immediate future. Let it glean from the various representatives of the farm organizations who may appear before the Standing Committee on Agriculture their ideas on how the program is working. After it has gained one or two years' experience of the program, let it tell parliamentarians what amendments it thinks ought to be made to the act, in order to make it more equitable for producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this amendment put forward by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) bears very heavily on some of the evidence we received from the farmers when we met with them over the week of meetings held in the west by the standing committee.
As I read the farm evidence and heard the farmers speak, they were putting forward a philosophy that when things were going well for the farmers they wanted to put more into the fund, and when things were going badly for them, they hoped they could put less into the fund. This is what I think the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is trying to put forward. However, in amending the government's legislation the best he could come up with was a 2 per cent constant levy.
In support of what the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) said earlier, I suggest very strongly that if the government had the wits that it should have had when it saw what the farmers were saying, it should have changed this variable levy from the way it has it, and reversed it.
At the present time under the government legislation, whenever the fund is doing well-in plain language there is a lot of money in the fund-and collecting too much interest from the government, it reduces the levy. Whenever the fund is doing poorly and there is not enough money to meet the interest requirement that the federal government loans to it, it raises the levy.
What the government has done in this legislation is the exact opposite of what the farmer wants. The farmer would not mind paying more money into the fund when he has the money, in the hope that he would not have to pay as much in when he does not have it. This is the philosophy of the motion of the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre that we support. However, the way it comes out in his amendment, he wants a fixed levy year in and year out. This makes the proposal of the hon. member for Moose Jaw very practical and acceptable. He is proposing that as soon as possible after you put this bill in you see if you can work out a proposal to make it a variable levy, and reverse it to the variable type of levy you now have.
I agree that that approach is better than what the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is proposing. However, I come back to the basic criticism that this proposal made by the hon. member for Moose Jaw, which is acceptable to the farmers much more than what the government is proposing and what the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is proposing, will only work if it is an individual plan. An individual farmer then knows that if he puts more money in, he individually, some time in the future, will get more money than he needs. This buttresses the feeling of the Progressive Conservative party on this legislation. If this legislation is going to work and do any good, it must
|Mr. Towers.]
eventually be wiped off the books and replaced by the type of stabilization income legislation which is based on the individual farmer.
I would like to emphasize this to the government members even though we cannot do too much about it at this particular stage of the bill's procedure through the House. In this debate they have heard it clearly debated by the hon. member for Moose Jaw and the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre. On the basis of philosophy the government's position is the worst position of all.
We are supporting the government position because at least in the mathematics of the scheme it is closer to what we want, which is a variable type of levy. However, the variation should be in reverse. It does not do much good to propose this at this stage, but at least any person who reads this debate will know the difference.
In essence, we will support the government position because it is a variable. On the basis of the mentality that they use in the civil service to judge these plans, it is more actuarially sound. However, it does not meet what the farmer wants. The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre is trying to get what the farmer wants, but does not know how to do it. We have proposed ways in which it can be done. However, to make it work, I suggest it will have to be made into an individual plan.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments on this. The Conservatives have said that they will support the government. The government position is not to have this on an individual basis. If there is to be an increase in the levy obviously it should be in a good year when the farmer is capable of making the payment, and not the reverse. It is stupid to say that because the farmer is having difficulty we will raise the levy. The members of the Conservative party see some merit in making it equal, so that it will at least not work in reverse.
I may have failed to realize something in the same way as did the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). It is my opinion that the way it works is that where the expenses are the highest, you have the highest levy, and where your income is the highest you have the lowest levy. That seems to be a complete reversal of stabilization. You make the highest payment when you have the least money and the lowest payment when you have a lot of money. That seems to be backwards. I cannot see any reason why the Conservatives are not in favour of stabilizing it so that we understand what happens from year to year, and we can look at the over-all payout.
The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) referred to the individual farmer. If the government were not so pigheaded, that is the way it would be operated.
We heard from the Manitoba deputy minister of agriculture, Mr. Janssen, a very astute economist and very practical person in terms of agriculture. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain may be interested in knowing that he suggested this should be on an individual basis. He said that in Manitoba all they had to do was add another three columns to their crop insurance program because they had already worked out the inputs into the cost of production. They were also aware of the inputs to the
November 28, 1975

income side. This is all worked out. All they need to do is add another three columns and they will be able to keep the books for the federal government at absolutely no administrative cost. This would mean that the more you put into the program, the higher your withdrawals could be. It would in effect change this to an income stabilization insurance rather than the net income .that we are trying to stabilize for all agriculture.
If we were really interested in individualization we would be concerned about the individual pay-in, the levy. This could be varied. I am sure the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain would agree that in that case the higher a person's income the more he would be paid-it would be a cash flow related to the situation of the individual farmer rather than one affecting the whole of western Canada, or at least that part which is covered by the legislation before us. I am sure most members would agree that this would be a more logical type of stabilization program upon which to embark.
I should not be surprised if the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) agrees with me that we are not likely to accomplish much with this bill. There is not much merit either in defeating it or in passing it. It is not really important one way or the other. It really affects the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) most because, being of German descent, he had the idea a long time ago that he would do something about stabilization and now he intends to do it, even if it is only to give a title to a bill. I have no doubt he is aware that if it is the intention to stabilize farm income in any effective way it would be necessary to call for heavy deductions when income is hfgh and reduce the levy as income falls. Then, when income reached a certain level we would begin making a payout. Thus, over a ten year period, we would have stabilized income at a certain level. But this is not what is being done.
My hon. friend, through trying to make the best of a bad arrangement, said we would stabilize the levy so that at least the same amount is paid all the time. This is an accepted practice. We have always done this in the past. A farmer who insures his barn pays the same amount whether he is expecting it to burn down or not. If we are to operate on this basis let us at least keep the levy stable so that farmers know what it is. To make the levy highest just when the farmer is reaching the point of a payout is an odd way of bringing about stabilization. It seems to me there must be a break-even point at which the payout would equal the premium.
The amendment is a good one though, because it equalizes the premiums as between good years and bad years. Anyone familiar with farming is aware that when the net cash flow decreases to a point at which costs are higher than receipts, farmers go to the government and to all government agencies asking for moratoria on the payments due on their land, machinery, and so on. Parliament has provided such a moratorium on a number of occasions, and we asked the farmers to make two payments on their land, machinery, and other debts when their cash flow was sufficiently high to enable them to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make three points briefly in response to the comments made on this motion. First the point raised by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) and others about the provisions in the bill to ensure the actuarial soundness of the plan. Actuarial soundness is very much adhered to here, and that is why the provisions to which he and others referred have been included.
I have been asked to predict what the rate is likely to be in the future, say, five, 10 or 15 years down the road. Let me point out that the bill does provide for the establishment of an advisory committee of producers with a mandate to look at anything in the legislation, or in the regulations and their administration, to ensure the plan is functioning well and in the best interests of the grain producers. That advisory committee could well look into the level of levy rates applicable. Indeed, I hope they could take this matter under early advisement. At any rate, provision has been made for the consideration of this question of fees paid by producers.
I wish to make one comment about the individualization of the plan. It seemed to me that in the course of our discussions in the committee stage two different concepts of individualization were advanced. One of them was put forward on behalf of the New Democratic Party, and observations of a similar vein were made by the National Farmers Union. What they were talking about boiled down to a plea for a kind of guaranteed income provision. Such a proposal is really quite different from a plan to stabilize proceeds from grain production. A guaranteed income scheme may be something that is a very laudable objective [DOT] for the future, but it does not particularly or peculiarly relate to the grain industry. It is a concept which, I suggest, embraces broad social policy; it is not one of narrow economic import having to do with one particular economic activity, namely, the grain industry.
On the other hand we have a proposal for individualization, which is the complete reverse. I think the hon. member for Moose Jaw as well as one of the witnesses before the committee, if I am not mistaken the Manitoba Farm Business Association, referred to the keeping of individual accounts, and this is something quite different from a guaranteed income program. If I may paraphrase the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), it boils down to a situation where each individual farmer bets against himself and his own abilities. This is quite different, I suggest, from the proposal that some of the New Democrats and others who appeared before the committee made.
My only comment about this final approach of keeping individual accounts is that, from the best investigation that we have been able to make in calculating what this

means in terms of government payments in and payments back to producers, the level of payment provided under the plan would be considerably less than that which is presently proposed in the legislation. This is why that approach has not been adopted.
To return to the major point, this amendment would take away from the actuarial soundness of the plan, and for that reason alone I would thank hon. members of the opposition for agreeing with us that this particular proposal should be defeated.

Personally I would have preferred something a little more specific in the amendment which would provide that parliament shall debate that report for a period of two or three days. I hope my confidence is not misplaced in that the government will see to it that the report not only is submitted to parliament but that it will ask for a reference of the report to the Standing Committee on Agriculture so that the committee can review the report and make an assessment with regard to the efficacy of the program, reporting back to parliament in respect of any changes which should be made to the program. This amendment would provide the avenue by which to do this. We must leave it to what we hope are the good intentions of the government in respect of this legislation.

I predict that the minister himself after that experience, and the report he makes to parliament, will be anxious to make some pretty fundamental changes to the legislation because, unless I miss my guess, a large number of grain producers after being in the program for two or three years will decide it is not really accomplishing what all of us desire, namely, the stabilization of the net farm income from grain sales. It will not accomplish this for those who need it the most, the small and the middle sized farmer. It will not make too much difference to the well-to-do large farmer. Our concern must be for the small and middlesized farmer who has the most difficult row to hoe when his net income drops drastically in two or three years out of every five or six years. Mr. Speaker, I do not think there will be any question about the government's willingness to accept this amendment because I believe when the three years are up the amendment will be redundant. There will be a new government sitting on the right of Mr. Speaker, which will bring in a proper income stabilization bill based on the right of the individual farmer to have an income stabilization fund into which both he and the government can contribute.
This bill is primarily and almost completely designed in the interests of the Department of Finance. If it brings any benefits to any farmer, they are only accidental. Therefore if we review it in three years we will probably find that the bill is bad.
I honestly hope that the viewpoint of the prairie farmers who are affected by this legislation will be accepted by people in all of Canada, in the rural areas as well as in the cities, and that we will get rid of this government which has been cluttering up the landscape for the last 12 years and not doing a single thing to help agriculture. All its members have given us is promises, roaring and bellowing, pawing of the ground, twisting and shaking of tails, but no record of performance.
This bill is a classical example. The rigidity and inflexibility of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board is so clearly apparent in this bill that it is a wonder his colleagues let him bring it back to the House. When we took this bill to farmers in western Canada, every group of farmers spoke in favour of an individual approach to this type of legislation, not this area payout concept under which you pay in a known amount but you do not know what your return will be. The kind of program that farmers accept today is one in which they know what they will pay in and what the return will be.
This bill is based on a complicated formula which the farmer will not be able to understand, and I doubt if there is a single person sitting in the House today who understands it. The only person who seems to understand the bill clearly is the minister himself, but when he says he understands it I really become worried.
So the first point I want to make is that we should accept the motion which calls for a review of the legislation in three years to try to improve it. But I hope and trust that three years from now a new government will be sitting on the other side which will get rid of all this complicated stuff and simply put forward a bill under which farmers will pay in their dollar, the government will pay in its contribution, and farmers will know what they will get when they need it because they themselves will decide what they want, and they will not be able to take out any more than they have put in. Under this type of individual approach the farmer will accept the program, and the government will benefit from it. Because farmers will get their money during periods when the economy is poor, it will do a lot to stabilize farm incomes in this country.

Farming is no longer a small item in the economics of our country. Today farming is a large item in the total income, and 10 or 15 years from now it will play an even larger part than it does today. Certainly by the end of the century the great resource industries of Canada will be many times greater than they are today.
If the government does not move now to stabilize incomes, not only of grain farmers but of all producers whose income goes up and down in wide fluctuations, the country will suffer. This bill was supposed to be an effort on the part of the government to try to stabilize this volatile grain activity. I will suggest right now that we must do our best to try to improve the program to make it acceptable to farmers so that they know what return they will get on the money they paid in. When they buy crop insurance, which is an insurance against weather, they know on an actuarial basis that is sound what they must pay in, and they know what they will get out of it.
According to this bill, farmers will get paid under a formula. Some year when they need the money desperately, they will not get it because the formula will say they are well off, and in other years when farmers have all the money they need, they will receive a payment because the formula will say they are broke.
This formula is just academic nonsense put into legislation which we in the House have to swallow. I certainly support the idea of reviewing it in three years, but it would be simpler to throw it out in three years' time when we form a new government and put something better in its place.

NON-SMOKERS RELIEF ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE RELIEF TO TRAVELLING NON-SMOKERS
speechtext:
that Bill C-242, respecting relief to non-smokers in transit, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to note that Bill C-242 has finally come before the House of Commons for debate. We are to discuss a measure respecting relief to non-smokers in transit.
The purpose of this bill, as set out in the short and long title, is to give relief to travelling non-smokers by stipulating that ?ailways, planes and buses under federal jurisdiction be required to provide them with separate seating accommodation, since there is medical evidence to the effect that secondary smoke inhalation not only causes distress to the non-smoker but could jeopardize his health, particularly if he suffers from heart disease or a respiratory ailment.
The purpose of this bill is simply to insist that nonsmokers actually have rights, that they are not second-class citizens and that they should not be forced to breathe
November 28, 1975

in somebody else's tobacco smoke. Obviously my bill, which specifically seeks to protect non-smokers by requiring that all air, marine, rail and road carriers under federal jurisdiction be required to provide non-smokers with separate seating accommodation, will not by itself guarantee the rights of non-smokers, for we again come up against the old problem of jurisdiction, and I think it is generally agreed that most of the legislative efforts on behalf of non-smokers must come at the provincial or municipal level. Nevertheless, this bill does strike at an area which is within federal jurisdiction and should, hopefully, set an example as a step in the right direction.
I would like at the outset to pay tribute to the former member from Surrey-White Rock, Barry Mather, who introduced a similar bill during the last parliament. I had the pleasure of serving with the former member on the Health, Welfare and Social Affairs committee during the twenty-eighth parliament and I came to know his deep concern for the subject. I am sure he would be extremely pleased by any action this House may deem to take with regard to providing relief to non-smokers.
This bill should not be interpreted as an anti-smoker or anti-smoking bill. It is not designed to try to prevent those people who wish to smoke from smoking, nor is it an attempt even to warn those who do smoke about the dangers of smoking. The Department of National Health and Welfare has for the last several years been conducting a program in this area. Bill C-242 is concerned solely with the non-smoker and the effects tobacco smoke has on him. For years almost no attention was paid to the plight of non-smokers and, indeed, the non-smoker himself did little or nothing in his own defence.
In the past few years we have seen a drastic change in attitude. No longer are non-smokers suffering in silence. The numerous non-smoking groups and their spin-offs which are now peppered across Canada and in the United States are testaments to this fact. These groups such as ASH, action on smoking and health; FANS, fresh air for non-smokers; GASP, group against smokers pollution; and the Non-Smokers' Rights Association were not even in existence before 1970; but now every province has at least one such group actively operating.
Undoubtedly one of the main reasons for this tremendous growth of militancy among non-smokers has been recent scientific studies which have shown tobacco smoke to be injurious to the health and a source of distress and illness not only to smokers but also to non-smokers. The effects of tobacco smoke and of the pollutants it contains on non-smokers can be influenced by many factors, such as the amount of pollutants found in the air; the ventillation available for the removal or dispersion of smoke; the proximity of an individual to the source of pollution; the length of exposure to the pollutants; or the health of the person so exposed. It is therefore impossible to say what the effect of tobacco smoke will be with regard to a particular individual. However, broad generalizations are possible.
Besides the general discomfort suffered by many individuals exposed to an atmosphere contaminated with tobacco smoke, diminished vision, short breath upon exertion, psychologic stress on patients with heart diseases, and allergic and irritative reactions may result.
Smoking Ban
Perhaps one of the most important sources of information on the effects of tobacco smoke on non-smokers has been a yearly report of the United States department of health, education and welfare on "The Health Consequences of Smoking", commonly referred to as the Surgeon General's report. The 1975 report which has been just released devotes an entire section to what the report refers to as "Involuntary Smoking."
Although the report discusses the subject using the most technical medical terminology, one point was made which I feel is very pertinent to this debate today, that is, that a survey conducted on symptoms experienced by travellers on both military and commcercial aircraft showed that over 60 per cent of the non-smoking passengers and between 15 per cent and 22 per cent of the smokers reported being annoyed by other passengers smoking, even though the aircraft were well ventillated and the level of measurable pollution low. This really confirms something which I long suspected, that is, that tobacco smoke in many cases is found to be annoying even by those who smoke. For this reason I believe that most smokers are themselves sympathetic to the kind of legislation this bill proposes.
I know that a number of hon. members, including the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), wish to speak this afternoon on this subject, so I will conclude my remarks not wishing to be accused of talking out my own bill. However, I would like to add that if members should decide to send my bill to committee, this would provide the opportunity for both members and ordinary citizens who have expressed a keen interest on this subject to make their contribution.
Finally I want to mention my intention of putting forward a couple of amendments to the bill as it now reads. These would cover responsibility for enforcement and penalties, and also a provision to ensure a reasonable minimum size for the non-smoking area. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would again like to stress my belief that this type of legislation is not only wanted, indeed demanded, by many non-smokers today, but is also completely acceptable by most of those who do smoke. Finally, Mr. Speaker, I happen to be a non-smoker, and will therefore be affected as much as any by this legislation.
