Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to have the opportunity today to take part in the debate on this very important bill that has been presented by the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson). I have known the hon. member for many years prior to the time that both of us came to this House. It is interesting to note that the concept of the bill provides some balance in terms of recognizing rights, using that word in the broad sense.
The bill, and I think the hon. member put it very forcibly, recognizes that non-smokers are not second class citizens. They have a right to comfort in terms of travel and in the use of accommodation. The bill implicity recognizes the fact that there are some in the community who use tobacco and who, by legislative enactment in terms of the areas within which this bill is designed to operate, might have that right, again using that word in a broad sense, taken from them.

November 28, 1975
Smoking Ban
It is very interesting that this bill should have the balance it does. I commend the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore for displaying this sense of balance and justice.
The hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore is a very distinguished member of the bar of the province of Ontario. For approximately two years I had the very distinct privilege of living in the same house as the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore. I found him at all times concerned about the rights of his neighbours. His habits were sometimes strange. He was somewhat nocturnal. He used to come in at varying hours of the day and night and would awaken all of us when he came in. However, he recognized that those of us who did not have the same habits should indulge ourselves in awakening him the next morning. He never chastised us. On all occasions he was a very balanced, hard-working individual. He has carried that into the House of Commons. I particularly commend him today with regard to the balance in terms of rights which this bill represents.
There are members of the House of Commons who adversly feel the effects of tobacco. We who smoke, and I have to identify myself as one who smokes, have to recognize this among our colleagues. The hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) is known far and wide for his delicate nasal passages. I am always prepared not only to recognize his right to speak but his right to breath in comfort, and to participate in the work of the committees of this House in comfort. That is a right we should recognize.
We cannot legislate good manners. We cannot legislate consideration for others. However, the way in which this bill has been presented goes some way in the public sense of indicating the concern of this, the highest court in the country, in recognizing certain basic rights.
It is interesting to note that Air Canada and CP Air have in relatively recent times adopted the practice of recognizing the right to comfort of non-smokers. This bill, balanced as it is, will further that cause.
I have received a large number of letters from my constituency expressing interest in this kind of legislation. I do not want to gainsay the efforts of the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore, but enforcement will be a problem. I am glad that amendments will be considered.
Many of my constituents have expressed great concern about this problem of recognizing one's right to comfort in a public place. I have brought this interest to the attention of the minister. I have a large number of letters. I do not intend to read all of them. However, I wish to refer to a letter from the office of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) replying to some earlier correspondence with regard to support of this kind of legislation.
Referring to my constituent, the executive assistant to the minister commended my constituent for her interest in the creation of non-smoking areas in air terminal buildings, and indicated that this has been recognized by the Minister of Transport. My constituent was further advised that the Director of Administration and Research had indicated that the matter was being studied by the department. However, there was a certain amount of hesitancy expressed in the letter as follows:

It should be emphasized that there is no quick or easy solution to this problem.
I suggest that all hon. members, whether they smoke or not, and whether they accept or do not accept the hon. member's statement about the injurious quality of tobacco both to the user and those in close proximity it really makes no difference. I suggest that all hon. members should support this legislation. This is a step in the right direction because it considers certain basic rights, the right to comfort, and the right to enjoy a public place without inconvenience or danger to health, if there is a danger in terms of a person being in close proximity to a smoker.
Having a firm knowledge of the backgroud of the hon. member who proposed this piece of legislation, his concern for the rights of others in terms of his work at the bar, his work as a trained and highly qualified social worker, his work as a municipal politician before coming to this place, and now knowing him as I know him here, I commend him for the foresight he has had and the great public spirit of concern he has exhibited in bringing forth this piece of legislation. I am happy to support it.

subtopic: NON-SMOKERS RELIEF ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE RELIEF TO TRAVELLING NON-SMOKERS
speechtext:
I should like to put a few facts on record for the benefit of the House and of the public generally, though I want to be sure I do not talk out the hon. member's bill. For more than a decade the Department of National Health and Welfare, in co-operation with other groups, has conducted a nation-wide program aimed at warning the smoker and those considering picking up the habit about the effects of smoking. In fact, I wrote to hon. members a couple of days ago telling them that we have a few of these buttons available for them to wear, or for others to wear. You will note that I am wearing one today. However, until recently little attention was paid to the effect of smoke on others in a room or area. Now these people have begun to draw public attention to their predicament and it is evident they should be protected in some manner.
At first the public tendency was to shrug off the nonsmoker as a nuisance minority. Some 70 per cent of the people in Canada are non-smokers. That estimate, of
Smoking Ban
course, includes children, who can also be harmed by inhaling tobacco smoke produced by others. Based on the 1967 U.S. National Health Survey there are probably at least three million Canadians suffering from a pre-existing susceptibility to cigarette smoke.
Non-smokers have formed a number of local groups in Canadian centres to promote the control of tobacco smoke. I understand there are some representatives of such groups in the gallery today. They suggest designating smoking and non-smoking spaces, smoke breaks during long meetings, and placing smokers nearest ventilation exhausts and non-smokers nearest ventillating air outlets, among other such techniques. The Department of National Health and Welfare together with various interested organizations and voluntary groups is also calling public attention to the plight of the non-smoker. Last spring the deputy ministers of my department sent a memo to each employee urging voluntary tobacco smoke control techniques in confined or crowded spaces. We hope there will soon be general acceptance of such practices.
Scientific testing has provided evidence of problems connected with the inhalation of smoke by non-smokers, so the people concerned have a legitimate complaint. The evidence indicates that individuals with asthma, allergies, advanced emphysema or advanced coronary arterial disease can be seriously troubled by inhaling cigarette smoke, especially in closed environments over a period of time.
As well, a smoke-filled room can often cause short term eye irritations to contact lens wearers. Moreover, preliminary studies indicate that respiratory ailments are more common among children whose parents smoke than among those whose parents do not. Another study has reported that infants in their first year of life are more prone to bronchitis and pneumonia when parents smoke.
Let me pose this question. If any hon. member was about to enter into a confined space-room, plane, bus, car or boat-where he would have to remain for some length of time-and was told in advance that the space contained nicotine, tar, carbon monoxide and other toxic gases, would he feel up to staying there? Would he enjoy a meal in such an environment? Yet time after time people are compelled to do something very similar, whether they smoke or not.
I should also like to call attention to studies of the chemical composition of tobacco smoke which have shown the presence of numerous toxic compounds, among them many irritants and cancer-producing substances. These compounds are sent into the air wherever tobacco is smoked. Their most objectionable emissions occur when the lighted tobacco is left to smoulder between puffs. The irritating, harmful substances in this sidestream smoke hover in the air and the non-smoker cannot help but inhale them. The non-smoker does not produce any of the pollutants, yet he must live with them, or try to.
There is one fact which bears further attention. The closer a non-smoker sits to a smoker, the greater the amounts of such pollutants as carbon monoxide and oxides of nitrogen he is exposed to. To a person who is allergic to the elements of tobacco smoke and to persons suffering from such ailments as asthma or emphysema, this concentration of smoke substances may be not only uncomfortable but agonizing. Even to healthy individuals, tobacco
9568

Smoking Ban
smoke hovering around their faces can be more than annoying. It can produce eye and nose discomfort, coughing, nausea or headache, or interfere with breathing. For the non-smoker sitting next to a smoker in an aircraft, train or bus, there may be no escape.
With transportation facilities more and more catering to family travel, we must also consider the small children. They should be protected from the chemicals in tobacco smoke, particularly when they are subjected to them in hours of travel.
How can all this be dealt with? Substantial ventilation can reduce the levels of irritants and noxious elements in confined areas. But ventilation costs money because of the added heating or cooling required, and it does not remove the damaging chemicals rapidly enough to relieve all sensitive non-smokers.
Some smokers are considerate and will curb their habit when they know they are in the company of non-smokers, and in particular in the company of those who indicate that tobacco smoke disturbs them, or brings them harm. There are smokers who will abstain when they are in a room or on a public vehicle because they themselves cannot tolerate the discomfort of sitting in a pall of tobacco smoke. But not enough can be accomplished by a simple appeal to the smoker. Unfortunately many of them are unresponsive to the need of the non-smoker to breathe uncontaminated air. Therefore there is a definite need for regulation of smoking in public places.
Some air carriers already designate areas for non-smokers. Early in the summer of 1974 Air Canada increased the number of "no smoking" seats on its aircraft. Depending on the number of seats and type of aircraft, the seats devoted to non-smokers were increased from 43 to 50 per cent. Air Canada said this increase came as a result of passenger demands.
At the present time "no smoking" areas are set up and policed by the carriers themselves. Recently the Civil Aeronautics Board of the United States expressed the belief that such self-imposed rules of the carriers were not an adequate remedy and that the voluntary efforts to segregate non-smokers and smokers were not effective. They reported receiving many letters in which passengers objected to being told that the non-smoking section of a plane was full, or being seated in a non-smoking section only to find no effort was made to prevent smoking by any of its occupants. On top of that, a joint survey by federal bodies in the United States reported more than 60 per cent of non-smokers who used air travel said they were bothered by tobacco smoke and urged either a ban on smoking or segregation of non-smokers and smokers on commercial flights.
Considerable correspondence received by non-government and government agencies in Canada and the United States has urged the complete banning of smoking on carriers. This correspondence did not come from cranks. The writers are genuinely concerned with their own comfort and health, as well as with the comfort and health of all who may be adversely affected by smoke. None the less, the U.S. Civil Aeronautics Board observed that, just as the attitudes of many smokers appeared to be insensitive to

the rights of others to be relieved of the annoyance and discomfort caused by smoking, so does the attitude of many non-smokers appear to be insensitive to the rights of the smokers.
After all, smoking is a lawful activity and to deprive smokers of this right could cause them severe discomfort. The U.S. board did not believe that the discomfort caused by smoking aboard aircraft could be reasonably dealt with by an absolute ban. The board believed that the segregation of smokers and non-smokers could establish an equitable balance. Consequently, on May 7, 1973, the U.S. Civil Aeronautics Board adopted a regulation requiring certificated air carriers to provide designated no smoking areas aboard their aircraft.
The U.S. Interstate Commerce Commission subsequently enacted a similar regulation respecting smoking on interstate passenger carrier vehicles. That arrangement appears to be the purpose of the hon. member's bill, Bill C-242.
I might add that some problems that could arise from such legislation should be considered in committee. For example, the bill calls for separate accommodation where smoking will be prohibited. It must be clearly indicated that this should not be interpreted as requiring any operator to permit smoking of cigarettes, cigars or pipes aboard the vehicle. Another problem could occur when the plane, train, bus or ship is faced with peak travel periods. At times like this it is quite possible that the number of seats available to either the smokers or non-smokers in the vehicle will not be enough to meet the demands. When such shortages occur there must be nothing to prevent the attendant-steward, stewardess, conductor or driver-setting up a temporary exchange of seats to achieve the correct balance.
A passenger must be given every opportunity to know of the existence of areas where smoking will not be permitted. For example, a passenger planning to travel by commercial aircraft must be advised when he makes his reservation that a non-smoking area is available in the aircraft. When he reaches the airport and checks in, his preference should be made known to the attendant. Then, when the attendant makes the customary announcements before take-off, specific reference should be made to regulations that exist regarding smoking and to the specified areas for non-smokers, what the regulations mean, and how they operate.
The procedure outlined here could be expanded by a variety of other means and be made known to the travelling public. In the 1969 report of the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs on tobacco and cigarette smoking, it is observed:
Your committee recommends that, out of consideration for the majority of Canadians who do not smoke, a gradually increasing number of no smoking areas or sections be provided in places or facilities used by the general public.
The committee noted there was increasing public recognition of the rights of non-smokers.
Attention should also be paid in legislation of this kind to the situation in smaller commercial vehicles, and I am glad that the hon. member has said he will entertain amendments on this particular subject.
The advantage for smokers of separate accommodations are twofold. The first is freedom from the increasing number of objections from non-smokers. In other words,
November 28, 1975

they would be assured of hassle-free smoking areas. Secondly, a smoker who is trying to quit the habit would be able to obtain social support for his changed lifestyle by using no smoking areas wherever they are available.
My department believes that there is a need for legislation in this area. While it cannot speak for other ministries which may be concerned with or even involved in this matter, there has been no objection to date to such legislation raised from those contacted. As I have said, Mr. Speaker, we have confidence that extensive benefits will result from legislation such as is outlined in Bill C-242.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too should like to congratulate the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) on his courage in bringing forward this bill. I do not know whether he polled his constituents to find out the proportion of non-smokers to smokers; one would hope that he had not and that it was purely on the principle involved and his interest in the subject that he has introduced this bill.
I join him in his recollection of the former hon. member for Surrey-White Rock and his long campaign. I note that when that constituency changed its politics it held firm to the non-smoking principle in sending the present member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) to this House.
There are many aspects to a bill such as this. It is easier to present the matter in the form of a bill, and one feels that it might have tremendous public acceptance, but one cannot always tell. I recall the moves made by the former premier of the province of British Columbia to ban the advertising of cigarettes and alcohol in publications in that province, and the great outcry that arose as a result of a move that I suspect he felt was going to meet with tremendous public acclaim. Once in effect, the reaction was other than what he expected.
I am a little concerned about this question of separate accommodations. It would seem simpler and more economic to ban smoking altogether, particular on air flights that are of fairly brief duration these days. The existing situation on Air Canada, for example, leaves something to be desired because there is no partition separating the eighth row from the ninth row, so the cut-off point between smoking accommodation and non-smoking is rather arbitrary.
Having listened to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) I think we might end up by dividing accommodation in aircraft of necessity into four separate compartments-first class smoking and non-smoking, and economy class smoking and non-smoking. This might add considerably to the expense of altering the aircraft. One would have to be reassured in this regard and perhaps an amendment could indicate just what would be acceptable to the mover of this bill as separate accommodation.
It is essential that we know what penalties are envisioned here because certainly enforcement is the key. I know it cannot be left up to the non-smoker to defend himself because very often a situation arises where the smoker is a very powerful and burly person while the non-smoker is not, and therefore there is a hesitancy to object vigorously to the presence of the smoker. I find that
Smoking Ban
far too often the staff of the vehicle or the plane will evade the responsibility and fail to be firm with some rather flagrant breaker of the rules.
I have heard a person in the non-smoking section ask the attendant if he could smoke, and the attendant has said to him that he may do so if no one objects. In that case the person proceeds to light up and the non-smokers are faced with the onus of preventing something that has already been allowed by the staff of the mode of transportation. So it is essential that there be enforcement, and that penalties are provided and are seen to be imposed and carried out.
I do not wish to be accused of talking out this bill. I think the categories covered here generally are satisfactory. There might be some difficulty in the case of a shared taxi to Hull because this would involve a very small vehicle. Again some passenger aircraft are very small.
There is one serious omission. I think the mode of transportation that can impose perhaps the severest penalty on the non-smoker is the elevator. In this institution, the House of Commons, I find that a vigorously puffed cigar in one of our elevators is about as extensive a hazard to one's health as one can be subjected to. I suggest the hon. member might give some thought to that very small but terribly confined form of transportation which is such as essential part of our life these days.

subtopic: NON-SMOKERS RELIEF ACT MEASURE TO PROVIDE RELIEF TO TRAVELLING NON-SMOKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no danger of my talking out the bill because I wish to go on record in support of it. However, I have one qualification. The bill does not go far enough. It is about time the House of Commons started to give a little leadership in respect of what I consider to be a very serious health hazard in this country.
The statistics given this afternoon point out the dangers in respect of smoking and the necessity for education of our young people in respect of the repercussions of smoking. In looking at the bill, and having thought about it for the past few days, I would say that the phrase "separate seating accommodation" gives me some cause for concern as to whether or not any realistic form of separation can be developed, especially on airplanes.
As the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston) pointed out a moment ago, the fact that smoking is permitted in row number nine but not in row number eight does very little for the person sitting in row number eight, or whatever the arbitrary line is, because of the very nature of smoking. If we do not put up a physical separation I have some doubt, speaking as one of many members of the House of Commons who have experienced the long suffering of air travel, about there really being sufficient help given to non-smokers.
As I think about the whole question, as I often do in my worst moments while being trapped in a seat beside, or even in, a smoking section, I have to consider which is the greater right-and I hope the committee will give a little thought to this-the freedom from smoke or the freedom to smoke. It seems to me that in modes of transportation the rights are irreconcilable because of the very nature of the beast.
I would say that if I were to give an opinion on this in the committee I think the freedom from smoke is a greater right. Therefore when I said a moment ago that the bill

November 28, 1975
Smoking Ban
does not go far enough what I have in mind is that I should like to see some experiment in which no smoking at all would be permitted. I have seen far too many examples of children becoming sick, and non-smokers and people with allergies being inconvenienced because they could not get into the non-smoking section of a plane since it is too small. Even having in mind what the minister just said about the non-smoking arrangements being enlarged, nonetheless they are too small.
I can assure you from bitter experience, Mr. Speaker, that very often the non-smoking section is filled up first. Even if one boarded the plane at a reasonable time one often ends up sitting in the smoking section. So I have some reservations about separate accommodation unless there is a physical separation involved. I doubt that this will happen, that is, that there will be consideration given to flights with no smoking permitted. This brings back the question of the greater right. There are some great questions at stake here. I hope the committee will give these serious consideration.
Finally, one of the things that will happen is that the public will become concerned about the effects of smoking as the committee begins its hearings. I believe some consideration should be given to the accommodation of patrons of a restaurant, people in theatre lobbies and, as the hon. member who just spoke mentioned, elevators. There is also the matter of smoking in hospitals. There are numerous cases in which members of the public are more or less forced to accommodate themselves to a given situation.
There is also the educational aspect of what we are discussing here. I think we must help more Canadians realize not only the dangers of smoking but also how the rights of non-smokers have been trampled on for far too long. It is about time we took some positive action in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I see we are running out of time and I would certainly not want to be accused of talking out this bill. However, I would simply want to add to what has been said, being
myself an addicted smoker-up to two or three packs of cigarettes a day-that I can now say that it is quite true that smoke-I will be older Sunday so I feel I must make a small confession today-is really damageable, that it is really unpleasant to go in public vehicles, by plane or train, and have to smell the smoke that people just blow in your face.
I share the opinion of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) about the efforts that his department is undertaking to carry out a greater education campaign to prove to people that it is really damageable to smoke. I share the reserves of my hon. friend and colleague from Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche) when he says that the bill perhaps does not go far enough but I think it is a step in the right direction and I join all my hon. colleagues on this Friday afternoon to congratulate our colleague from Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for having had the wisdom to introduce this legislation. I think we will agree to vote this bill this afternoon.
